title: Cardiovascular Pathogens
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the organisms that infect the heart and great vessels: the bacteria of infective endocarditis, Trypanosoma cruzi, the tick-borne bacteria Borrelia burgdorferi and Rickettsia rickettsii, the hemorrhagic fever viruses, the myocarditis viruses, and three older infections that still appear on boards (diphtheria, tuberculosis, and syphilis). Board questions give a Gram stain, a bench test, a vector, or an exposure and ask for the organism, or name the organism and ask which structure or virulence factor explains the disease. If you can connect each organism's structure and life cycle to the tissue it damages, you can reason through most questions in this area.
prerequisites: Gram stain, bacterial cell wall structure, and catalase and coagulase tests
Viral classification by genome type, strand sense, and envelope
Fc receptors, opsonization, complement, and type I interferon
Valve and conduction system anatomy (CV-4, CV-7)
Aortic wall histology and the vasa vasorum (CV-2)

connections.how: That chapter covers the vegetations, acute versus subacute course, and peripheral signs of endocarditis caused by the organisms described here.
The T-cell phase of viral myocarditis and the immune basis of rheumatic fever continue the story of direct viral and bacterial injury told here.
Lyme disease, Chagas disease, and diphtheria all damage conduction tissue, so the AV and bundle branch blocks of CV-7 appear as their findings.
Tuberculous pericarditis is a leading cause of the constrictive physiology described in that chapter.
Syphilitic aortitis and rickettsial vasculitis are vascular infections whose mechanisms are taught here.

terms.def: A mass of platelets, fibrin, and microorganisms attached to a heart valve or the endocardium.
A microbial surface molecule that binds a host molecule and lets the organism attach to tissue.

A Staphylococcus aureus product that converts fibrinogen to fibrin, either by activating prothrombin (free coagulase) or by binding fibrinogen on the cell surface (bound coagulase, or clumping factor).
A S. aureus surface protein that binds the Fc region of IgG and so blocks opsonization and complement activation.
A community of microorganisms enclosed in a self-made polymer matrix and attached to a surface, which protects them from phagocytes, antibodies, and antibiotics.
An organism that grows only on enriched media or under special conditions, and usually slowly.
An organism that can multiply only inside a host cell because it depends on host metabolites or energy.
The flagellated, extracellular form of Trypanosoma cruzi that circulates in blood and invades cells but does not divide in humans.
The rounded intracellular form of Trypanosoma cruzi, without an external flagellum, that multiplies by binary fission inside host cells.
Repeated change in an organism's surface antigens that keeps it ahead of the host's specific antibodies.
Increased viral entry into Fc receptor-bearing cells when antibodies bind a virus without neutralizing it.
Concentric thickening of the intima of small arteries that narrows or closes their lumen and makes the tissue they supply ischemic.

sections.title: The major endocarditis bacteria: morphology and virulence factors

blocks.text: Infective endocarditis begins when organisms in the blood attach to a heart valve and multiply in a vegetation. Each organism's adhesins decide which valves it can colonize, and its toxins decide how fast the valve is destroyed. The four classic organisms are gram-positive cocci, separated by their arrangement on Gram stain, by catalase (made by staphylococci, not by streptococci or enterococci), and by coagulase.
Staphylococcus aureus

Staphylococci divide in several planes and form grapelike clusters. S. aureus is catalase and coagulase positive. Bound coagulase (clumping factor) binds fibrinogen, and free coagulase activates prothrombin so that fibrin coats the organism and hinders phagocytosis. Clumping factor and fibronectin-binding proteins let S. aureus attach to fibrinogen and fibronectin on minimally injured or even normal endothelium and then enter endothelial cells. Protein A binds the Fc region of IgG, holding antibody in an orientation that cannot opsonize or fix complement. Pore-forming alpha toxin and tissue-degrading enzymes then destroy leaflets within days. These factors explain why S. aureus causes acute endocarditis on previously normal valves, why abscesses and perforation are common, and why it leads in people who inject drugs, in whom skin bacteria reach the tricuspid valve first.
Viridans streptococci

Streptococci divide in one plane and form chains. Viridans streptococci (for example S. sanguinis, S. mutans, and S. mitis) are normal mouth flora with alpha hemolysis, a partial greenish hemolysis produced when their hydrogen peroxide oxidizes hemoglobin. They are optochin resistant and not bile soluble, which separates them from Streptococcus pneumoniae, the other alpha-hemolytic streptococcus. They invade poorly and need an abnormal valve. Turbulent flow across a scarred or congenitally abnormal valve injures the endothelium, and a sterile platelet-fibrin deposit forms. During the brief bacteremia of tooth brushing or dental work, strains that make dextran, a glucan polymer built from dietary sucrose, stick to this deposit and become buried in it, shielded from neutrophils. A slow-growing, weakly toxic organism gives subacute disease over weeks to months.
Enterococcus faecalis and Staphylococcus epidermidis

Enterococcus faecalis is a catalase-negative bowel commensal in pairs and short chains that carries the Lancefield group D antigen, grows in 6.5% NaCl and bile, and hydrolyzes esculin, all signs of a hardy organism. It reaches the blood from the urinary or gastrointestinal tract, often after instrumentation in older adults, and causes subacute endocarditis; surface adhesins and biofilm help it attach, and it is intrinsically resistant to many antibiotics. Staphylococcus epidermidis is a coagulase-negative, novobiocin-sensitive skin commensal of low virulence. On a prosthetic valve, pacemaker lead, or catheter it secretes a polysaccharide adhesin and builds biofilm that excludes neutrophils and antibodies. It is the classic cause of prosthetic valve endocarditis in the first year after surgery, but a single positive blood culture is often skin contamination.

blocks.predict: Why can S. aureus infect a normal tricuspid valve when viridans streptococci rarely infect a normal valve?
blocks.explain: S. aureus adhesins bind fibrinogen and fibronectin on minimally injured endothelium, and its toxins destroy tissue. Viridans streptococci depend on dextran binding to a platelet-fibrin deposit already present on a damaged valve.

blocks.text: Culture-negative endocarditis is endocarditis, by clinical and echocardiographic findings, with no growth in routine blood cultures. The most common reason is antibiotics given before cultures were drawn. The rest come from organisms that grow slowly, need special media, or live inside cells, and each has a recognizable exposure.
HACEK organisms

HACEK names fastidious gram-negative rods and coccobacilli that are normal oropharyngeal flora: Haemophilus species (mainly H. parainfluenzae), Aggregatibacter (formerly Actinobacillus and some Haemophilus species), Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens, and Kingella kingae. They need enriched media and added CO2 and grow slowly, which is why they were classically culture-negative, although modern automated blood culture systems usually recover them within about 5 days. They enter the blood from the mouth, often with dental disease, and tend to form large, friable vegetations that embolize.
Coxiella burnetii and Bartonella

Coxiella burnetii, the agent of Q fever, is a small gram-negative obligate intracellular bacterium that multiplies inside the acidic phagolysosome of macrophages. A spore-like small-cell form survives drying for long periods, so people are infected by inhaling dust or aerosols contaminated with the birth products (placenta, amniotic fluid) of cattle, sheep, and goats; no vector is needed. Acute infection is usually mild or causes pneumonia or hepatitis, but in people with damaged or prosthetic valves, vascular grafts, or weak immunity the organism persists and causes chronic endocarditis with small or absent vegetations. It does not grow in routine culture, so diagnosis rests on serology, with high antibody titers against phase I antigen marking chronic infection.

Bartonella species are fastidious, facultatively intracellular gram-negative rods. Bartonella quintana is carried by the human body louse and causes endocarditis in people experiencing homelessness or alcohol use disorder, and Bartonella henselae comes from cats through scratches or cat fleas. Diagnosis uses serology, PCR, or silver-stained valve tissue.

Inhaled aerosols from livestock birth products
Does not grow in routine culture media
blocks.caption: Less common causes include Brucella, Tropheryma whipplei, Legionella, and fungi.

blocks.text: Streptococcus gallolyticus and colon cancer

Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly Streptococcus bovis biotype I) is a group D streptococcus of the colon. Like Enterococcus it is bile-esculin positive, but unlike Enterococcus it does not grow in 6.5% NaCl. A colorectal adenoma or carcinoma disrupts the mucosal barrier and lets the organism into the blood, and it appears to colonize tumor tissue more readily than normal mucosa. A large share of patients with S. gallolyticus bacteremia or endocarditis have colorectal neoplasia, so isolating it calls for evaluation of the colon even without bowel symptoms. Whether the bacterium promotes tumor growth or only exploits the tumor is still debated.

blocks.title: Identifying a group D organism from the bench tests
blocks.text: Blood cultures from an older adult with a new murmur grow gram-positive cocci in chains that are catalase negative and nonhemolytic. The isolate hydrolyzes esculin in the presence of bile but does not grow in 6.5% NaCl. Step 1: chains and a negative catalase test mean a streptococcus or an enterococcus. Step 2: growth on bile esculin means a group D organism, either Enterococcus or S. gallolyticus. Step 3: failure to grow in 6.5% NaCl excludes Enterococcus, so the organism is S. gallolyticus. Step 4: its source is the colon, and its presence suggests a colorectal tumor that should be looked for. Had it grown in salt, the answer would be Enterococcus, with a urinary or bowel source.

sections.title: Trypanosoma cruzi: life cycle, transmission, and Chagas disease

blocks.text: Trypanosoma cruzi is a flagellated protozoan that causes Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis). It is endemic in rural Mexico, Central America, and South America, where triatomine bugs (reduviid or kissing bugs) live in the cracks of poorly built houses. The bugs feed at night, often on the face, and defecate during or soon after the blood meal. The parasite is in the feces, not the saliva, so the bite itself does not transmit it.

blocks.title: Life cycle of Trypanosoma cruzi
steps: Bug ingests blood trypomastigotes during a blood meal
In the bug midgut, epimastigotes multiply
In the hindgut, metacyclic trypomastigotes form and pass in feces
Feces rubbed into the bite wound, conjunctiva, or mucosa
Trypomastigotes invade host cells and become amastigotes
Amastigotes divide by binary fission in the cytoplasm
Amastigotes become trypomastigotes and the cell ruptures
Blood trypomastigotes infect new cells or a feeding bug
blocks.caption: Multiplication occurs only as epimastigotes in the bug and as intracellular amastigotes in the human.

blocks.text: The two human forms divide the work. The trypomastigote is the flagellated extracellular form that circulates in blood and invades cells but does not divide, unlike the African trypanosomes, which multiply in blood. After entry the parasite escapes its vacuole into the cytoplasm and becomes an amastigote, a rounded form without an external flagellum that divides until it fills the cell. Amastigotes then change back into trypomastigotes and rupture the cell, so parasite numbers rise only inside host cells. Favored cells are macrophages, cardiac myocytes, smooth muscle, and neurons of the enteric plexuses. Entry through the conjunctiva gives painless swelling of one eyelid (Romaña sign), and entry through skin gives a local inflammatory nodule (chagoma).

Because trypomastigotes circulate and amastigotes persist in tissue for life, the parasite can spread without the bug. Blood transfusion and organ transplant from an infected donor, passage across the placenta, food or juice contaminated with bugs or their feces, and laboratory accidents all transmit it, which is why chronic carriers far from endemic areas matter to blood banks and transplant programs. Oral outbreaks deliver a large inoculum and tend to cause severe acute myocarditis.

The acute phase lasts several weeks to about 2 months, with many trypomastigotes visible on a stained blood smear, and is usually mild. Most people then enter a lifelong indeterminate phase with few circulating parasites, so diagnosis depends on serology. Over decades about 20 to 30% develop chronic disease. Persisting amastigotes and the inflammation they provoke destroy myocytes and replace them with fibrosis, producing dilated cardiomyopathy, a thin apical aneurysm that can hold thrombus, and conduction disease, typically right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block. Loss of myenteric neurons leaves the esophagus and colon unable to relax and propel their contents, so they dilate into megaesophagus and megacolon.

sections.title: Tick-borne bacteria: Borrelia burgdorferi and Rickettsia rickettsii

blocks.text: Borrelia burgdorferi

Borrelia is a spirochete, a long, thin, helical bacterium whose flagella lie in the periplasm between its inner and outer membranes. Their rotation turns the whole cell like a corkscrew, letting it move through connective tissue. The outer membrane lacks classic lipopolysaccharide and is rich in lipoproteins, and the cell is too thin to see well on Gram stain, so it is shown with Giemsa, Wright, or silver stains. Its genome is a linear chromosome plus many linear and circular plasmids, which carry most surface protein genes. The vectors are Ixodes ticks (Ixodes scapularis in the eastern United States, Ixodes pacificus in the West). Larval ticks acquire Borrelia from the white-footed mouse, the main reservoir; nymphs transmit most human infections; deer feed adult ticks but are not a significant reservoir.

blocks.title: Borrelia surface switching from tick to host
steps: Unfed tick gut: Borrelia expresses OspA, anchoring it to the gut
Blood meal warms the tick and supplies nutrients
OspA falls, OspC rises, and spirochetes multiply
Spirochetes migrate to the tick salivary glands
OspC binds tick salivary protein Salp15, shielding the spirochete
Injection into skin, usually after 36 to 48 hours attached
In the host, VlsE variation keeps specific antibody behind
blocks.caption: The switch and migration take time, so a tick removed within the first day rarely transmits infection.

blocks.text: In the host, recombination moves segments of silent vls cassettes into the expressed vlsE gene, so the surface lipoprotein VlsE keeps changing and antibody to the old version no longer binds. Spread through skin produces erythema migrans, and spread through blood carries it to the heart, joints, and nervous system. In Lyme carditis, spirochetes and a lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltrate involve the myocardium and conduction tissue, most often producing AV block, usually at the AV node, that can change degree within hours and usually resolves as inflammation subsides.
Rickettsia rickettsii

Rickettsia rickettsii, the cause of Rocky Mountain spotted fever, is a small gram-negative coccobacillus that stains poorly with Gram stain and is shown with Giemsa or Gimenez stain. It is obligate intracellular because it imports ATP and other metabolites from host cytoplasm and cannot make enough of its own coenzyme A and NAD+. Dermacentor ticks (the American dog tick and the Rocky Mountain wood tick) are both vector and reservoir, passing the organism to their offspring through the eggs. Despite the name, most US cases occur in southeastern and south-central states.

Outer membrane proteins (OmpA and OmpB) bind endothelial cells and trigger uptake. The bacterium lyses the phagosome, multiplies in the cytoplasm, and polymerizes host actin into a tail that pushes it into the next endothelial cell, so infection travels along small vessels of the skin, brain, lungs, and kidneys. Injured endothelium becomes leaky and procoagulant, causing a small-vessel vasculitis with edema, loss of intravascular volume, hypotension, and platelet consumption. The rash, which appears a few days after fever begins, starts as macules on the wrists and ankles, spreads to the trunk and onto the palms and soles, and becomes petechial as vessel damage progresses.

blocks.title: Borrelia burgdorferi versus Rickettsia rickettsii
rows: OspA to OspC switch, VlsE variation
Actin-based spread from cell to cell
blocks.caption: Ixodes carries Borrelia; Dermacentor carries Rickettsia rickettsii.

blocks.predict: Why does removing an Ixodes tick within the first 24 hours greatly lower the risk of Lyme disease?
blocks.explain: Borrelia in an unfed tick sits in the gut expressing OspA. It must switch to OspC, multiply, and reach the salivary glands before injection, which usually takes 36 to 48 hours.

sections.title: Hemorrhagic fever viruses: flaviviruses, filoviruses, and enhancement in dengue

blocks.text: Flaviviruses and filoviruses are enveloped single-stranded RNA viruses that can cause viral hemorrhagic fever, a syndrome of fever, vascular leak, bleeding, and shock. Their genomes are read in opposite ways. A positive-sense genome is itself mRNA, so it is translated directly and naked genome RNA is infectious. A negative-sense genome is complementary to mRNA, so the virion must carry an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase to copy it, and naked genome RNA is not infectious.

blocks.title: Flaviviruses versus filoviruses
rows: Positive-sense ssRNA; one polyprotein cut by proteases
Humans (dengue); monkeys in the forest cycle (yellow fever)
Contact with blood and body fluids; no vector
Monocytes and dendritic cells; hepatocytes (yellow fever)
Macrophages, dendritic cells, then endothelium and hepatocytes
blocks.caption: Both end in endothelial leak and coagulopathy.

blocks.text: Yellow fever and dengue

Both are spread mainly by Aedes aegypti, a day-biting urban mosquito; yellow fever also circulates in a forest cycle among monkeys and forest mosquitoes in Africa and South America. Yellow fever virus targets the liver. Hepatocytes in the midzone of the lobule (zone 2) die by apoptosis and appear as eosinophilic Councilman bodies, and loss of hepatocyte function causes jaundice and reduced clotting factor synthesis, which with endothelial damage produces bleeding, including black vomit, and renal failure. Dengue virus has four serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4) and infects dendritic cells, monocytes, and macrophages. Severe dengue is a plasma leak syndrome that peaks as fever falls, with hemoconcentration, low platelets, and shock; the secreted viral protein NS1 adds to leak by damaging the endothelial glycocalyx.
Antibody-dependent enhancement in dengue

One serotype gives lasting immunity to itself but only brief cross-protection against the others. Years later, antibodies from the first infection still bind a different serotype but cannot neutralize it. The coated virus attaches to Fc gamma receptors on monocytes and macrophages, which take it in more efficiently than the virus could enter alone, and this route of entry also dampens interferon responses. Viral load rises, and cross-reactive memory T cells add a burst of cytokines that worsens leak. The same mechanism explains severe dengue in infants who still carry waning maternal antibody at their first infection.

blocks.title: Reading the labs of a second dengue infection
blocks.text: A traveler had mild DENV-1 infection 4 years ago and now has fever after another trip. On day 5, as her fever breaks, she becomes lightheaded; hematocrit has risen from 40% to 48%, and platelets are 40,000/µL (normal about 150,000 to 400,000/µL). Step 1: worsening as fever falls marks the critical phase. Step 2: a rising hematocrit without fluid loss means plasma has leaked from the vessels. Step 3: a different serotype now meets nonneutralizing DENV-1 antibodies, which carry it into Fc receptor-bearing monocytes, raising viral load and cytokines. Step 4: low platelets add bleeding risk to shock.
Ebola and Marburg

Fruit bats are the reservoir; Rousettus bats are proven for Marburg virus, and bats are strongly suspected for Ebola virus. Humans are infected through contact with bats or infected wild animals, then spread the virus by direct contact with blood and other body fluids, including those of the dead, so caregiving and burial practices amplify outbreaks. Virus can persist for months in semen. The glycoprotein GP mediates entry into macrophages, monocytes, and dendritic cells first. Ebola VP35 blocks type I interferon induction and VP24 blocks interferon signaling, so replication outruns innate defense, infected dendritic cells fail to activate T cells, and bystander lymphocytes die by apoptosis. Infected macrophages release TNF, IL-6, and tissue factor, which triggers disseminated intravascular coagulation, and later infection of endothelium and hepatocytes adds leak and clotting factor loss.

sections.title: Viral myocarditis: coxsackie B virus and other cardiotropic viruses

blocks.text: Myocarditis is inflammation of the myocardium with myocyte injury, and in high-income countries viruses are its most commonly identified cause. Coxsackie B virus (serotypes B1 to B6) is the classic example. It is an enterovirus in the picornavirus family: a small, nonenveloped (naked), icosahedral virus with a positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome. Without an envelope it resists stomach acid, bile, and drying, so it spreads mainly by the fecal-oral route, and also through respiratory secretions, mostly in summer and fall. It replicates first in the pharynx and intestinal lymphoid tissue and reaches the heart during viremia.

blocks.title: Coxsackie B virus from gut to dilated heart
steps: Fecal-oral or respiratory entry; replication in gut lymphoid tissue
Viremia carries virus to the heart
Virus binds DAF (CD55), then CAR at intercalated discs
Genome translated into one polyprotein
Protease 2A cleaves eIF4G and dystrophin
Sarcolemma tears; myocytes die and release troponin
T-cell inflammation and fibrosis; possible dilated cardiomyopathy
blocks.caption: Direct viral injury in the first days is followed by immune-mediated injury over weeks.

blocks.text: Entry depends on the coxsackie-adenovirus receptor (CAR), a transmembrane protein of the immunoglobulin superfamily that sits in tight junctions and, in the heart, at intercalated discs. Many strains first bind decay-accelerating factor (DAF, CD55) on the cell surface, which helps deliver them to CAR. CAR is abundant in the developing heart and is expressed again in injured myocardium, one reason neonatal coxsackie myocarditis is severe. Inside the cell the genome is translated from an internal ribosome entry site into one polyprotein, which the viral proteases 2A and 3C cut into functional proteins. Protease 2A also cleaves eIF4G, shutting off cap-dependent host translation, and cleaves dystrophin, which links sarcomeric actin to the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex in the sarcolemma. Without that link the membrane tears under contractile stress, the same structural failure that causes cardiomyopathy in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

Myocyte loss reduces contractility and releases troponin, and inflamed myocardium is electrically unstable, causing arrhythmias and ST and T wave changes. The T-cell response that follows clears virus but also kills infected myocytes (CV-16), and persisting viral RNA with disrupted dystrophin can leave a dilated ventricle. Coxsackie B often inflames the pericardium as well (myopericarditis, with pleuritic chest pain and a friction rub) and also causes pleurodynia and aseptic meningitis.
Other myocarditis viruses

blocks.title: Other viruses found in myocarditis
rows: Fiber protein binds CAR; important cause in children
Binds P antigen (globoside) on erythroid precursors and endothelium; injures small vessels
Latent in lymphocytes; can reactivate or be integrated into chromosomes
blocks.caption: Influenza virus, SARS-CoV-2, HIV, and hepatitis C virus are other recognized causes.

blocks.text: Parvovirus B19 and HHV-6 genomes are now among the most frequent viral findings in heart biopsies, but both are also found in hearts without myocarditis, so a positive result does not by itself prove that the virus caused the disease.

sections.title: Diphtheria myocarditis, tuberculous pericarditis, and syphilitic aortitis

blocks.text: Diphtheria toxin myocarditis

Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a club-shaped gram-positive rod that lies in V and L patterns, contains metachromatic (polyphosphate) granules, and forms black colonies on tellurite agar. It colonizes the pharynx without invading deeply. Only strains carrying a lysogenic beta-prophage with the tox gene make toxin, and the bacterial repressor DtxR blocks tox transcription when iron is plentiful, so toxin is made when iron is scarce. The toxin is an A-B exotoxin: the B portion binds the heparin-binding EGF-like growth factor precursor, the toxin enters an endosome, and acidification moves the A fragment into the cytoplasm, where it ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2 (EF-2). Protein synthesis stops and the cell dies.

Locally, dead epithelium, fibrin, and leukocytes form a gray, adherent pseudomembrane. Absorbed toxin reaches the myocardium and peripheral nerves. Myocarditis usually appears 1 to 2 weeks into the illness, often as the throat improves: myocyte degeneration and necrosis with relatively little inflammation cause AV and bundle branch block, arrhythmias, and heart failure, and it is a major cause of death in diphtheria. Demyelinating neuropathy follows later.
Tuberculous constrictive pericarditis

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an acid-fast rod whose mycolic acid-rich wall resists decolorization and survives inside macrophages. It usually reaches the pericardium by retrograde lymphatic spread from mediastinal (peritracheal and peribronchial) lymph nodes, or by blood. The cell-mediated response forms caseating granulomas and a fibrinous, often bloody effusion. As inflammation heals, the visceral and parietal layers fuse into a thick fibrous, sometimes calcified shell. Tuberculosis is the leading cause of constrictive pericarditis where it is common, especially with HIV, whereas idiopathic, postsurgical, and radiation causes predominate elsewhere.

The rigid shell fixes the total volume of the heart. Early diastolic filling is rapid until the ventricles meet the shell, then stops abruptly, producing a pericardial knock and a steep y descent in the jugular venous pulse. The inspiratory fall in intrathoracic pressure is not transmitted through the shell, so the extra venous return of inspiration cannot enter the right heart and jugular venous pressure rises (Kussmaul sign). Diastolic pressures equalize in all four chambers, and systemic venous congestion causes hepatomegaly, ascites, and edema.
Syphilitic aortitis

Treponema pallidum is a thin spirochete that is invisible on Gram stain and is seen by dark-field microscopy or silver stain. In tertiary syphilis, usually 10 to 30 years after untreated infection, treponemes persist around the vasa vasorum, the small adventitial arteries that nourish the outer media of the thoracic aorta.

blocks.title: From vasa vasorum endarteritis to aortic aneurysm
steps: Treponemes persist in the adventitia around vasa vasorum
Lymphocyte and plasma cell cuffs surround the vessels
Intimal thickening (obliterative endarteritis) narrows vasa vasorum
Outer media becomes ischemic
Elastic fibers and smooth muscle lost; patchy scarring
Weakened ascending aorta and arch dilate
Aneurysm, aortic regurgitation, coronary ostial narrowing
blocks.caption: The aortic wall fails from ischemia of its media, not from direct destruction by the organism.

blocks.text: The ascending aorta and arch are affected because they depend most on vasa vasorum. The intima over the scarred media wrinkles into a tree-bark pattern and may calcify. Dilation of the aortic root stretches the valve ring and causes aortic regurgitation, narrowing of the coronary ostia causes angina, and a large aneurysm can compress the trachea, esophagus, or left recurrent laryngeal nerve.

blocks.predict: Why does syphilis cause aneurysms of the ascending aorta, while atherosclerosis mainly causes aneurysms of the infrarenal abdominal aorta?
blocks.explain: Syphilis injures the vasa vasorum, which are richest in the thoracic aorta. Atherosclerotic intimal thickening impairs diffusion from the lumen, which matters most in the infrarenal aorta because it has few vasa vasorum.

integration.text: The organisms in this chapter sort by the cardiovascular structure they reach and how they reach it. Endocarditis bacteria arrive through bacteremia from the skin, mouth, gut, or urinary tract and attach to valves by adhesins; Trypanosoma cruzi, Borrelia, and coxsackie B reach the myocardium during parasitemia, spirochetemia, or viremia; rickettsiae and the hemorrhagic fever viruses injure endothelium everywhere; diphtheria toxin travels without its bacterium. Anatomy then predicts the findings: conduction tissue explains the AV blocks of Lyme disease, Chagas disease, and diphtheria, the vasa vasorum explain why syphilis targets the thoracic aorta, and the fixed pericardial shell explains constrictive physiology after tuberculosis.

Many lesions are produced partly by the host. T-cell attack drives the chronic phase of Chagas disease and the later phase of viral myocarditis, antibody plus Fc receptors drives severe dengue, and cytokines and tissue factor from infected macrophages drive DIC in Ebola. Organism-level facts such as reservoirs, vector ranges, and the proportion of infections that progress vary between sources and change with surveillance, so they are stated here as approximate, and the virulence factors named are the best established among many.

summary: S. aureus (clusters, catalase and coagulase positive) uses clumping factor, fibronectin-binding proteins, protein A, and toxins to destroy normal valves acutely, especially the tricuspid valve in injection drug use.
Viridans streptococci (chains, alpha-hemolytic, optochin resistant) use dextran to stick to platelet-fibrin deposits on damaged valves after dental bacteremia, giving subacute disease.
Enterococcus grows in 6.5% NaCl and bile and follows urinary or bowel procedures; S. epidermidis forms biofilm on prosthetic valves and devices.
Culture-negative endocarditis usually reflects prior antibiotics; otherwise think HACEK (oral fastidious gram-negative rods), Coxiella (livestock aerosols, serology), or Bartonella (body lice, cats).
S. gallolyticus is bile-esculin positive but does not grow in 6.5% NaCl, and its isolation calls for a search for colorectal neoplasia.

Trypanosoma cruzi is transmitted in triatomine bug feces and also by transfusion, transplant, the placenta, and food; nondividing blood trypomastigotes seed cells where amastigotes multiply, leading decades later to dilated cardiomyopathy, apical aneurysm, conduction block, megaesophagus, and megacolon.

Borrelia burgdorferi switches from OspA to OspC before transmission from Ixodes ticks (36 to 48 hours), varies VlsE in the host, and causes AV block; Rickettsia rickettsii from Dermacentor ticks infects endothelium and spreads by actin tails, causing vasculitis and a rash that moves from wrists and ankles inward.

Flaviviruses (positive-sense, Aedes-borne) cause yellow fever hepatitis with Councilman bodies and dengue plasma leak worsened by antibody-dependent enhancement; filoviruses (negative-sense, bat reservoir, body fluid spread) block interferon and trigger DIC.

Coxsackie B, a naked positive-sense picornavirus spread fecal-orally, enters through CAR and cleaves dystrophin and eIF4G with protease 2A; adenovirus, parvovirus B19, and HHV-6 also appear in myocarditis.

Diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates EF-2 and causes myocarditis with conduction block; tuberculosis causes constrictive pericarditis; tertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum and ascending aortic aneurysm.

verify: The proportion of patients with S. gallolyticus bacteremia or endocarditis who have colorectal neoplasia ranges widely between studies (roughly a quarter to over half); confirm whether NABNE expects a figure.
HACEK organisms are now usually recovered by automated blood culture systems within about 5 days; confirm whether NABNE still classifies them as culture-negative causes.
Coxiella grows in specialized cell-free research media; the board label obligate intracellular is kept.
Chronic Chagas disease is quoted as developing in about 20 to 30% of infected people (some sources give up to 30 to 40%); confirm the figure NABNE uses.
Borrelia transmission usually needs 36 to 48 hours of attachment; Rickettsia rickettsii transmission time varies and is not stated.
Lyme carditis frequency is given as about 1% of reported cases in recent US surveillance and up to about 4 to 10% in older series; not stated in the text.
The onset of diphtheritic myocarditis is given variably (from the first week to several weeks); this chapter uses the commonly cited 1 to 2 weeks.
Bats are confirmed as the reservoir of Marburg virus (Rousettus aegyptiacus) but remain the suspected, not proven, reservoir of Ebola virus.
The causal role of parvovirus B19 and HHV-6 genomes found in heart biopsies is debated; DAF (CD55) use as a coreceptor varies among coxsackie B strains.

Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms and named signs Romaña sign, Councilman bodies, and Kussmaul sign, and the molecular names Salp15, VlsE, VP35, VP24, and DtxR, or only the descriptive mechanisms.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: tcruzi-life-cycle (bug and human stages with the form at each step) and gram-positive-cocci-key (catalase, coagulase, hemolysis, optochin, bile esculin, and 6.5% NaCl branch points).
